hero.name: Priyanka
hero.who: a 17-year-old NEET aspirant in Kota who loses her study hours to reels

story.b: Priyanka moved from Jabalpur to a PG in Kota for medical entrance coaching. Every evening at seven, she sits down with her physics module, phone face down beside it. She only turns it over to check a doubt in the batch group. Then a friend's story catches her eye, then a reel, then a sale on kurtis. When she looks up, it is past nine and the module is still on page one. The Sunday mock test is three days away. Last week she deleted Instagram in anger and reinstalled it two days later. When her mother calls at night and asks how studies are going, Priyanka says fine, and then lies awake feeling guilty.

ask.q: Priyanka has deleted and reinstalled Instagram three times. What should she try to understand first?
o: Which phone setting would block apps completely
Why she reaches for the phone in the first place
How toppers manage to never touch their phones
ask.why: Blocking apps treats the phone as the whole problem, and she has already seen deleting fail. Comparing herself to toppers only adds guilt. Understanding what pushes her toward the phone, in the exact moment she reaches for it, is where lasting change begins.

chapters.take: Deleting the app is easy. Understanding why you reach for it matters more.

story.b: Priyanka keeps a stack of sticky notes by her books. Every time her hand moves toward the phone, she stops and writes one word for how she feels. After a week, the notes tell a clear story. Confused, when organic chemistry stops making sense. Scared, when she remembers her last mock score. Homesick, around ten at night, when the PG goes quiet and she misses her mother's dal. The phone was never the real problem. It was her escape hatch. So she starts dealing with the feelings directly. Confusing problems get a star and go to her teacher the next morning. And she fixes a proper call with her mother every night at nine thirty.

ask.q: Priyanka reaches for her phone right when a tough chemistry problem confuses her. What should she do in that moment?
o: Name the feeling, then deal with its cause, like marking the doubt for her teacher
Force herself to keep staring at the problem until it clicks
Allow a short scroll as a reward for trying
ask.why: The phone is just an escape from the discomfort of confusion. Staring harder leaves the feeling unresolved, and a reward scroll usually becomes an hour. Naming the feeling and handling its real cause, like noting the doubt, removes the reason to escape.

chapters.take: Distraction usually starts with a feeling. Deal with the feeling, not just the phone.

story.b: Priyanka tries something new. Every night before sleeping, she writes the next day's plan in her diary, and she includes fun. From eight thirty to nine, reels, guilt-free. Sunday evening, a film with her PG friends. Now when she watches reels at eight thirty, she enjoys them, because that is exactly what she planned. The surprise comes in her biology block. She catches herself spending forty minutes making colourful mind maps of a chapter she had planned to solve questions from. It looks like studying. It feels productive. But it is not what she decided to do with that hour. She puts the coloured pens back in their box and opens the question bank.

ask.q: During her planned question-solving hour, Priyanka spends forty minutes decorating notes. Is that traction or distraction?
o: Traction, because anything related to studies counts
Traction, because neat notes will help her later
Distraction, because it pulls her away from what she planned for that hour
ask.why: Traction means moving toward what you planned, not just doing something that looks useful. Decorating notes feels productive, but she planned to solve questions, so it pulled her away. Deciding beforehand is what lets her tell the difference honestly.

chapters.take: If you did not plan it, even useful-looking work can be a distraction.

story.b: Priyanka's old to-do list was long and hopeless: finish physics, revise biology, practise chemistry, call home, do laundry. Every night most of it carried over. So she buys a sheet of chart paper from the stationery shop near the coaching centre and draws her week as a grid. Coaching from eight to two. Lunch and rest till three thirty. Physics from four to six. Chai and a walk with her roommate. Biology from seven to eight thirty. Reels till nine. Call home. Sleep by eleven. Laundry on Sunday morning. When a friend asks her to go to the market on a Tuesday evening, she checks the grid and offers Sunday instead. The friend agrees.

ask.q: Priyanka's roommate keeps a long to-do list but never gets through it. What should she try?
o: Make the list longer so nothing is forgotten
Give each task a fixed time block in her day, including rest
Do whichever task feels easiest first to build momentum
ask.why: A list says what to do but not when, so tasks pile up and the easy ones always win. Giving each one a time block, including breaks, turns intentions into a schedule she can follow. The day stops being a string of fresh decisions.

chapters.take: Give every part of your day a time, and the day follows the plan.

story.b: Even with a timetable, Priyanka's phone keeps lighting up. The batch group has three hundred students and buzzes every minute. A cousin's wedding group sends dance videos all evening. Two shopping apps send sale alerts. She goes through every notification and asks if it truly helps her. Only two survive: her mother, and the coaching centre's official channel. She mutes the batch group during study blocks and checks it once, at eight thirty, for useful doubts. The wedding group stays muted until the wedding. She also sticks a small note on her door that says she is studying till eight thirty, and her PG friends start knocking less. The quiet evenings feel strange at first, then wonderful.

ask.q: Priyanka's batch group of three hundred students pings all evening, sometimes with useful doubts. What should she do?
o: Leave the group completely, even though it has useful doubts
Keep notifications on so she never misses anything
Mute it during study blocks and check it once at a fixed time
ask.why: Leaving loses the useful doubts, and keeping alerts on lets three hundred people decide when she is interrupted. Muting it and checking at a set time keeps the value while removing the constant pulls. Each alert should have to earn its place.

chapters.take: Question every ping. Keep only the alerts that truly help you.

story.b: Most days now go to plan. But on long Sunday revision days, when the hours stretch, Priyanka still slips. So she adds a few pacts. During long study sessions, her phone goes to her roommate's room, so checking it means walking down the corridor and knocking. She and her roommate agree that whoever checks a phone during a study block buys samosas for both from the stall downstairs. And she starts calling herself someone who does not touch her phone while studying. It sounds silly at first. But the next Sunday, when the urge comes during a tough chapter, the corridor feels very long and the samosas feel expensive. She stays at her desk and finishes the chapter.

ask.q: Priyanka still slips on long Sunday revision days. Which step would help most now?
o: Make a pact, like leaving her phone with her roommate until the session ends
Study even longer hours to make up for slipping
Feel guilty after each slip so she remembers next time
ask.why: With her feelings, plan and alerts already handled, a pact adds a final barrier at the weak moment. Studying longer gives distraction more time to win, and guilt often sends people back to the phone for comfort. Putting distance between her and the phone makes slipping harder.

chapters.take: A pact makes distraction harder exactly when your willpower is lowest.

story.b: Ten weeks later, Priyanka's mock scores have climbed steadily, not dramatically, but every Sunday a little higher. The chart paper timetable is soft at the corners and covered in ticks. She still watches reels at eight thirty, and she enjoys them more now, because she has earned them and they end on time. When her hand moves toward the phone at the wrong moment, she has learned to ask what she is feeling. Usually it is confusion, and the doubt goes to her teacher. Her calls with her mother at nine thirty are real conversations now, not quick lies. Her roommate has made her own chart paper grid, and the two of them owe each other far fewer samosas.

chapters.take: Focus came from understanding her feelings, planning her day and guarding her time.
